conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. My toe’s feeling a little better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. We’ll keep you on colchicine. Also, your BNP is high—2890—consistent with heart strain, but it’s been that high before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So my heart’s still struggling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s under stress, but you’re not fluid overloaded. We’re keeping your diuretic the same for now—torsemide once daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We reviewed your iron levels. You have iron deficiency anemia—ferritin is low. We’ll keep an eye on it, but no transfusion needed now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Anemia? I’ve been feeling tired, but I thought it was just everything else.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could be part of it. We’ll discuss long-term iron replacement with your primary doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well overnight. Heart rhythm stable, oxygen down to 1 liter, and your toe is improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel better. Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly tomorrow. We want to make sure you’re stable and understand your discharge plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What changes to my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Torsemide is now once daily instead of twice. All your other heart, diabetes, and COPD meds stay the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I thought I was on two doses of that water pill.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You were, but your weight is stable and you’re not retaining fluid. Once daily is safer and just as effective now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I can do that. And the insulin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Same as before—Lantus at night and sliding scale as needed. Your blood sugar was high the morning you came in, but it’s been controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I ate something sweet before I left the house. Won’t do that again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home today. Weight is 80.7 kg, lungs are clear, and your heart is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Weigh yourself every morning. If you gain more than 3 pounds in a day or two, call your doctor. Watch for shortness of breath, chest pain, or dizziness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And no drinking or cocaine, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It’s crucial for your heart and overall health. Your cardiologist will talk to you about the defibrillator when you’re ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. Thanks for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re setting up follow-up with your primary doctor and cardiologist. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check before discharge. Any chest pain, dizziness, or trouble breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I feel fine. A little weak, but okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s normal after being in bed. Keep moving slowly. Here’s your discharge summary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I’ll read it when I get home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And remember—call 911 if you pass out again or have severe symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I don’t want to go through that again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll help you stay out of the hospital. Take your meds, stay off substances, and keep your appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do my best. Thanks, doc.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee, one of the neurosurgery team. You're in the hospital after being found unconscious outside a building. You had a fall and hit your head.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I... I don’t remember anything. My head hurts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have a head injury. The scan shows bleeding in your brain on the left side, called a subarachnoid hemorrhage. There’s also a skull fracture behind your left ear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it is. Later that evening, another scan showed the bleeding got worse. There’s now a large clot in the brain with swelling pushing the brain to the right side.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We reviewed your case carefully. Because of your other health issues—like heart failure and lung disease—the risk of surgery is too high. We’re focusing on comfort and managing the pressure in your brain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I see...

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re still on the ventilator because you’re not breathing well on your own. We’re also watching your blood pressure and kidney function closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My chest feels heavy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray shows some fluid in the lungs, likely from heart failure. We’re giving diuretics to help reduce the fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We started you on insulin because your blood sugar was high. Your heart function is very weak—your ejection fraction is only 10%. We’re adjusting your medications carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had heart problems for years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we’re managing that. But right now, the brain injury is the main concern. Your family was contacted and they’re trying to understand the situation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve developed a fever. We took cultures and started antibiotics for pneumonia. The sputum grew Enterobacter, which is sensitive to the antibiotics you’re on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel hot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re treating the infection. Your white blood cell count is high, which confirms your body is fighting something.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your sodium level is rising. It’s now 150. We’re giving free water flushes to bring it down slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m thirsty.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know, but we have to be careful. Too much fluid too fast could worsen brain swelling. We’re monitoring closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The chest X-ray shows the pneumonia is getting worse. We’re continuing the same antibiotics. The nodules we saw might be from infection or fluid, but we’re watching.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it spreading?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The infection is in your lungs, but we’re treating it. Your body is weak from the brain injury, so it’s harder to fight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your neurological exam hasn’t improved. You’re not moving your right side, which suggests a stroke-like effect from the brain bleed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can’t feel my right arm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s due to the injury on the left side of your brain. Unfortunately, with the extent of the damage, recovery is unlikely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did another brain scan. The bleeding in the left side has slightly decreased, but the clot in the right frontal lobe has grown. The pressure in your brain is still high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s getting worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The overall situation remains very serious. The new bleeding adds to the damage. We’re focusing on keeping you comfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your family met with us yesterday. They understand your condition is not improving. They’re discussing what to do next.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I want to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But right now, you need the ventilator to breathe. Your body isn’t strong enough to do it on its own.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your kidney function is declining. BUN is 94, creatinine 1.5. We’re not giving certain medications to avoid further strain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My legs are swollen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s from fluid buildup due to heart and kidney issues. We’re balancing fluids carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re having trouble maintaining blood pressure. We started Levophed to support it. Your body is under a lot of stress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and your exam shows no response to pain. The brain injury is severe. We’ve made you DNR/DNI for now, pending your family’s final decision.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your family arrived. After discussion, they’ve decided to make you comfort measures only. We’ll stop the ventilator and keep you comfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The family is here with you. We’re going to remove the breathing tube now. You’re not alone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We are now terminating mechanical ventilation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Time of death is 15:44.
